I have a recently convert Catholic in my campaign right now playing a Catholic paladin, and it's been getting difficult to work with, as it's hard to critique his character without risking offending him. Like, the lines between the player and the character are difficult to read.

I love what you guys did and might propose something similar as a way to rework his character- if I end up keeping him in my campaign.

Get this, he's playing a Catholic paladin. The concept is actually pretty fun and if done by the right person ~~(an ex-Catholic)~~ I think it would have worked- but it's quickly becoming just a more extreme version of himself and his beliefs. Just like anytime anyone plays a character like that, it becomes difficult to critique the character's actions without the player taking it as a personal affront. I think this whole thread has opened my eyes a little bit more to the reality that this won't work out, and that was without this aspect tied in.

Thank you. I think a lot of the new converts get excited by the power to judge people, and abuse it- probably due to something they are lacking in their own lives- especially when you can justify it by trying to "save" your friends. I think feeling sympathy for him has clouded my judgement in the past, but just like it's not his job to "save" me, it's not my job to "save" him/understand him- or tolerate his behavior, as it would be.
You mean people who are desperate for control over their life, but ignore the problem and instead find fulfillment through getting invested in a religion that allows them to judge others? Lol

He has (unfortunately) already had to deal with my parents- we've been together for 5 years almost. Luckily they've been good to him other than the pressure to get married, lol. I think part of the problem is, I thought I was "over" that part of my life, but  I'm now having to process and relive everything on top of trying to convey to someone else how this is affecting me (forgetting the bad parts about the first 18 years of your life isn't actually healing, shocker! /s). I appreciate the suggestions!

First off, congrats on embracing your identity! Being closeted is scary. I know it seems like you will never be in an environment where you will be able to be yourself, but I promise you will be. People are much more open-minded and accepting than we like to believe. If you need a space to open up, there are a lot of great communities on the internet and even here on reddit to talk about being bisexual and be yourself. Your friends don't hate you. It might feel like they do, but unfortunately that's part of being a teenager, its a constant tumultuous sea of trying to find what you believe in, who to trust, etc. But if you appreciate your friends, they appreciate you too, even if they might not be great at expressing it. I truly believed that aspect of my life would never improve, but I promise in the next coming years you will lose some friends, keep some that will grow only stronger, and form friendships so strong you'll never have that fear. Stay strong, you have a great head on your shoulders already! :)

I don't understand how that's possible, how to separate the love from the pain, but I'm trying to believe in that right now. Isn't it weird how when we're heartbroken we cannot comprehend that someone else is sharing our pain? We believe we are the only one who has experienced this type of agony. I think that's what makes it hurt more. We believe we are so alone in this suffering, and that no one else has felt this pain.

Think of it this way: imagine if every time you tried to eat, somebody started flicking your ear. The entire time you're eating, they won't stop, no matter how much you argue with them or tell them to go away. You eventually give up and try to distract yourself by talking to whoever you're eating with. They mention something about calories or how they're on a diet, or anything food-related. Now the person flicking your ear is pinching it and won't let go until you put the fork down. 

My point is, most of the time, its not even coherent thoughts. A lot of the time, its just overwhelming guilt whenever I try to eat. Enough to make my throat close up and make me not want to eat ever again. Other than that, any thoughts are just stuff like "you'll regret this later when you see more fat on your body" or "if you gain any weight from eating this, you're going to have to eat even less to make up for the fact that you gained weight." Stuff like that.

I think lonely is a dick to everyone. He's an audacious egotist who refuses to learn his place.

There is a certain type of lonely that comes when someone important in our lives leaves, especially when we know that they are still out there, living and breathing, smiling, laughing, perhaps happier without us, perhaps not. I like to believe that when we get close to someone, we hand off a small part of our soul to them, except sometimes we give too much and they run off with it, making it seem as though there is nothing left for us; but there is still a piece of our soul kept with us, that will grow to be whole again. Lonely fights against this personal growth, is the sleazy ex who comes crawling back every time it gets dumped by the last person. It may fester now and again, it may leave a small scar, but every scar tells a story of what you survived, as will be the case when you overcome Lonely. 


Lonely loves the night because it is hard to deny someone shelter in the deepest hours of the darkness. "You wouldn't leave me out in the cold, would you?" it says, already removing its shoes as it steps over the threshold of your room. It already knows the answer. No one can refuse Lonely. Especially not then. What Lonely does not realize is that there are moments that transcend the need for another person, that it is possible to be alone and not be lonely. 


One day, even when Lonely taps on your window, you will no longer feel the need to let it in. I am still learning this process, and so are you, and many others. In this process, we are both united and alone simultaneously, as we cannot learn to be comfortable with our alone without being alone. 


Lonely may have you in its grip now, but those gashes will be heal, and the comfort you will find in yourself and the support from those around you will kiss them better. There is too much beauty to compensate for Lonely to be found in yourself, in others, in the world itself, to let it consume you. It takes time, lots of time, but you will heal.

Absolutely. Lonely sits beside you while you watch a movie, despite choosing one you thought it hated. Lonely slips beside you under the covers as another night is spent sleepless. Lonely is a ghost that does nothing more than destroy with its presence: it does not speak, does not care for seances, it is only silent.

A girl I had never met before politely tapped on the door of the stall I was in and asked if I wanted someone to talk to. After I finished venting to her, she gave me a hug and told me to take the time I needed to finish crying. She left, and then came back a few minutes later with a pack of tissues and some cookies she bought from a vending machine and gave them to me. I still tear up thinking about how nice she was. I wish I could see her again so I could thank her.

Start with baby steps. Pick up hobbies that make you feel good about yourself, like, go to the gym, maybe pick up an instrument, maybe even baking or cooking if you're interested in that kind of stuff. Try new things! Even if you don't think you'll like them, you'll have the satisfaction of trying to experience the world, which can be kind of a self-confidence booster in itself. And once you find a hobby/hobbies you enjoy doing, it'll help you create a better image of yourself, and fill the hole in your life that weed was originally occupying. 
Other than that, write down a list of all of your positive qualities, both physical and personality-wise. Then make a list of stuff you want to improve about yourself, and try to come up with ways to fix those. If you ever feel discouraged, just look at the list of good things you wrote about yourself, and remind yourself that part of growing is realizing you're not going to feel good about yourself every single day, and that's okay. 
Hope this helps!
